approach: Show the learner how much Spanish they can already read: identical and near cognates, the spelling patterns that disguise them, each word heard with its Spanish sound, then practice spotting and decoding them.
coverage: A cognate is a word that looks alike and means the same in two languages
Some cognates are spelled exactly like English: hotel, hospital, animal, chocolate, doctor
Many differ by a small change: restaurante, familia, importante, música, teléfono
Pattern: English st- at the start becomes est- (student, estudiante)
Pattern: ph becomes f and th becomes t (telephone, teléfono; theater, teatro)
Pattern: many English words gain a final -e, -o or -a (important, importante)
Cognates are said the Spanish way: hotel is oh-TEL
Not every word is a cognate: casa, perro and mesa must be learned

blocks.purpose: Defines a cognate and why it gives a beginner hundreds of words at once.

data.anchor: A cognate is a Spanish word that looks like an English word and means the same thing, so you can read it the first time you see it.
prerequisites: Spanish and English share thousands of words from Latin and from each other.
Some are spelled the same: hotel, hospital, animal, chocolate, doctor, actor, color, idea.
Most differ by a letter or two: restaurante, familia, importante, música, teléfono.
Always say them the Spanish way: clean vowels and a silent h.

trapReasons.0: It is spelled exactly like the English word, so it is tempting to say it the English way.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: A cognate looks English, so the brain reads it in English. But the spelling is Spanish, and Spanish rules decide the sound.
data.correctReasoning: Silent h, clean vowels: oh-TEL. The stress falls on the last syllable, as it does in most Spanish words ending in l.
data.recoveryTip: Read a cognate twice: once for meaning (English), once for sound (Spanish).

data.takeaway: Hundreds of Spanish words are English words in disguise: look past st- to est-, ph to f, th to t and an extra final vowel, then say them with Spanish sounds.

checks.rationale: Universidad is the cognate of university: the English -ity ending often becomes -idad in Spanish.
checks.hint: Think of a place where you study after high school.

checks.prompt: An English word starts with "sp", like "special". What usually happens to it in Spanish?
checks.answer: It gains an e at the start: especial
checks.rationale: Spanish words do not begin with s plus a consonant, so an e is added in front: special becomes especial, as student becomes estudiante.
choices: The s becomes a z: zpecial
It stays exactly the same: special
It gains an e at the start: especial

checks.rationale: Telephone becomes teléfono: ph turns into f and a final -o is added.
